summary: Aerodromes are listed in AIP AD. Get prior permission (PPR) before you go; tell your destination if you divert or will be 45 minutes or more late. Green Morse beacons mark civil aerodromes, red military. On the ground give way to landing traffic, turn right head-on, give way to traffic on your right. Declared distances: TORA, TODA (plus clearway), ASDA (plus stopway), LDA. Runway markings are white, taxiway yellow; threshold lights green, end lights red. Learn the signals-area symbols, holding point lines (broken side towards the runway), displaced thresholds, ATC light signals in flight and on the ground, and the main marshalling signals.
sections: What an aerodrome is
An aerodrome is any area of land or water used for aircraft to take off and land
Aerodromes fall into categories depending on their use
The AD (Aerodromes) section of the UK AIP holds the aerodrome directory: physical characteristics, local hazards and flying restrictions
Prior permission (PPR) and limits on use
Military aerodromes and civil aerodromes with an ordinary licence: prior permission to land from the aerodrome authority
Unlicensed aerodromes: permission from the owner or person in charge
PPR = prior permission required. Contact the operator or owner before departure, especially if no radio frequency is published
Landing without PPR is trespass. You may also miss safety information: a strip usable only one way or in certain winds, waterlogging, noise abatement procedures
Ignoring PPR can lead to an accident and the insurer refusing to pay, because you breached the ANO
Military aerodromes: PPR always before departure, and expect to need higher insurance cover
Civil use of military aerodromes is limited to their normal hours of watch and to aircraft on inland flights; some also limit the class of traffic (scheduled, charter or private)
None of these restrictions apply in an in-flight emergency. Aerodromes not listed in AIP AD may be used in an emergency or with the owner's or operator's permission
ANO rules at aerodromes: instruction, fuel, arrival and customs

Flying instruction (Article 209): at an unlicensed (or non-certified) aerodrome, instruction towards a pilot's licence or a flight test for one needs the operator to be satisfied the facilities are adequate, and the commander must not take off unless they are also satisfied
Fuel (Article 220): never use fuel you know or suspect is unfit; aerodrome fuel must be stored and sampled as the rules require
Avgas equipment at aerodromes is usually marked in red
Arrival: if you are expected somewhere, tell that aerodrome as soon as possible if you change destination or will be 45 minutes or more late, to avoid needless overdue action
Where possible, report to the aerodrome authority on arrival and before departure
Customs airports for international flights, with hours and special requirements, are listed in the GEN section of the AIP
Security (ICAO Annex 17)
Annex 17 covers aviation security
Aims: prevent unlawful interference with civil aviation, keep people safe, protect passengers and staff, and respond rapidly to any increased threat
Know the local security arrangements where you fly. Security is everyone's responsibility
Aeronautical light beacons
Fitted at various civil and military aerodromes. Expect them on at night, and by day in poor visibility, whenever the aerodrome is operating
Identification beacon: flashes a two-letter Morse group every 12 seconds, green at civil aerodromes and red at military ones
Aerodrome beacon: alternating flashes, usually white/white, less often white/green
An aerodrome beacon is not normally provided as well as an identification beacon
Moving on the aerodrome (Rules 12 and 13)
Do not taxi on the apron or manoeuvring area without the aerodrome authority's permission
Manoeuvring area: the part used for take-off, landing and taxiing, excluding aprons and maintenance areas
Apron: the paved area for loading and unloading, turn-rounds, maintenance and repair, and other approved uses that are not flight operations
Nobody may go onto any part of an aerodrome provided for aircraft without permission, unless it is a public right of way
Right of way on the ground (SERA.3210)
Whatever ATC has cleared, the commander must do everything possible to avoid colliding with other aircraft, vehicles or obstacles. The onus is on you
If an aircraft is being towed with its commander not on board, that duty falls on the person in charge of the towing vehicle
Aircraft on the ground give way to aircraft taking off or landing
Head-on: each turns right
Converging: the aircraft with the other on its right gives way, and does not cross ahead unless well clear (stop, or pass behind)
Overtaking: the aircraft being overtaken has right of way; the overtaker keeps out of the way until past and well clear (your textbook: keep clear on the left of it, so its pilot can see you)
Aerodrome Traffic Zones (ATZs)
Airspace around most UK aerodromes is designated an Aerodrome Traffic Zone, usually because of the amount of flying there
In an ATZ, keep radio (or other) contact with the aerodrome unit: ATC, AFIS or Air/Ground (see Rules of the Air)
The dimensions of an ATZ and the airspace around it are in the Airspace topic
Declared distances (TORA, TODA, ASDA, LDA)
Declared distances are agreed by the relevant authority (the CAA in the UK) and published in the AD section of the AIP
TORA (take-off run available): the runway length declared available and suitable for the ground run of an aeroplane taking off
TODA (take-off distance available): TORA plus the clearway, if there is one
ASDA (accelerate-stop distance available): TORA plus the stopway, if there is one. No stopway: ASDA = TORA
LDA (landing distance available): the runway length declared available and suitable for the ground run of an aeroplane landing. A displaced threshold shortens it
Trap: clearway goes with TODA (it is airspace you climb over), stopway goes with ASDA (it is ground you can stop on)
Aerodrome standards (ICAO Annex 14)
Annex 14 sets ICAO's standards and recommended practices for aerodromes: physical characteristics, layout, equipment, people and procedures
Contracting states try to conform to them under the Chicago Convention
Worth reading: CAP 637 (Visual Aids Handbook) and CAP 1535 (the Skyway Code)
Runway surface condition (GRF and SNOWTAM)
The Global Reporting Format (GRF) gives pilots runway surface conditions in one standard format worldwide
Dry: no visible moisture and not contaminated in the area to be used
Wet: any visible dampness or water up to and including 3 mm deep
Slippery wet: a wet runway where friction over a significant part has been found to be degraded
Contaminated: a significant part of the surface in use is covered by one of the eight contaminants: compacted snow, dry snow, frost, ice, slush, standing water, wet ice, wet snow
Reported for each third of the runway. A runway is contaminated when more than a quarter of at least one third is covered
For each third: a runway condition code from 0 (worst) to 6 (best), coverage (25, 50, 75 or 100%), depth in mm, and a description
Used all year: a SNOWTAM (a special NOTAM) reports or cancels hazardous snow, ice, slush or standing water, even with no winter weather

Reading a SNOWTAM, e.g. EGGP 03150045 09 2/5/5 50/75/75 04/NR/NR SLUSH/WET/WET: aerodrome; assessed 15 March 00:45 (MMDDhhmm); the lower runway number (09, so the report also covers 27 in use); codes, coverage %, depth (NR = not reported) and description for each third
Indicators, markings and signs (Annex 14 ch. 5)
Every aerodrome has at least one wind direction indicator, visible from aircraft in flight and on the movement area, and sited clear of disturbed air from nearby objects
A landing direction indicator, if provided, sits in a conspicuous place
Runway markings are white. Taxiway and aircraft stand markings are yellow
Mandatory instruction signs are white on a red background
Runway lights (Annex 14 5.3)
Threshold and wingbar lights: fixed, unidirectional, green towards the approach
A runway with edge lights also has runway end lights, ideally at least 6
End lights sit at right angles to the runway, as near the end as possible and no more than 3 m outside it
End lights are fixed, unidirectional, showing red along the runway (towards an aircraft rolling towards them)
Trap: green threshold lights face the approach, not the runway; the red end lights face the runway
Obstacle lights and marking (Annex 14 6.3)
Low-intensity obstacle lights on vehicles: flashing yellow (emergency and security vehicles excepted)
High-intensity obstacle lights: flashing white
Obstacles within 15 km of an aerodrome are normally lit at night
A fixed obstacle 45 m or less in height, width and length: a single steady red light on its highest point. Larger ones get extra red lights outlining them
Obstacles hard to see by day are painted in alternating bands or a chequered pattern of red or orange and white
Signals area: direction and surfaces
Some aerodromes have a signals area near the tower, for messages without radio: signals laid on the ground are read in flight; signals hoisted on a mast are read on the ground
White T: take off and land parallel with the shaft, towards the cross-arm (into wind), unless ATC authorise otherwise
White disc at the head of the T: the directions of landing and take-off do not necessarily coincide. A black ball on the mast means the same
White dumb-bell: on the ground, keep to paved, metalled or similar hard surfaces
Dumb-bell with a black strip across each disc: take off and land on a runway, but other ground movement is not confined to hard surfaces
Dumb-bell with a red L: light aircraft may take off and land on a runway or on the area marked by a white L
Signals area: circuit direction and warnings
Red and yellow striped arrow, bent through 90° round the edge of the signals area and pointing clockwise: turns before landing and after take-off are to the right
Variable circuit: a rectangular red flag on the mast = left-hand circuit, green flag = right-hand (the same as navigation lights: red port, green starboard)
Red square with one yellow diagonal: the manoeuvring area is in poor state; take special care approaching and landing
Red square with a yellow diagonal cross: landing is prohibited, and likely to stay so
White H: helicopters take off and land only in the designated area (marked by a much larger white H)
Double white cross and/or two red balls on the mast, one above the other: glider flying is taking place. A much larger double cross marks an area for gliders only

Yellow cross: the tow-rope dropping area. Tow-ropes, banners and the like are picked up or dropped only at an aerodrome, as the aerodrome authority directs, or in that area flying in the landing direction
Signals on paved runways and taxiways
Two or more crosses, arms at 45° to the centreline, no more than 300 m apart: that section is unfit for aircraft. White on a runway, yellow on a taxiway
Orange and white markers no more than 15 m apart mark the boundary of an unfit part of a paved runway, taxiway or apron (a base board with a slatted upright board, striped orange-white-orange)
Holding point: parallel yellow lines across the taxiway, usually two continuous and two broken. No part of an aircraft or vehicle goes beyond them towards the runway without ATC permission
The broken lines are on the runway side. Coming off the runway you meet the broken lines first, and need no clearance to cross
Older holding points may be white, or one continuous and one broken line
Markers on unpaved manoeuvring areas
Aerodrome boundary: orange and white striped wedge-shaped markers (like long wheel chocks) no more than 45 m apart, with flat orange and white markers on structures on the boundary
Unserviceable unpaved area: the same wedges alternating with square flags of orange and white triangles; the bad ground inside is marked with white crosses
Unpaved runway or stopway boundary: flat white rectangles, flush with the surface, no more than 90 m apart
A stopway is a prepared rectangle beyond the runway end, in the take-off direction, where an aircraft can stop after an abandoned take-off
White L: part of the manoeuvring area for light aircraft only
White T on the left of a runway (seen from the landing direction): the runway to be used. With no runway, it gives the take-off and landing direction
White cross at each end of a runway: landing is dangerous and the aerodrome is for storage only
White cross and a single white bar at each end, at a disused aerodrome: fit for emergency use only. Such runways are not safeguarded and may be obstructed
Displaced thresholds
The threshold marks the start of the usable runway for landing. It is normally piano keys; the runway number is the direction rounded to the nearest 10° (09 = 090°)
A threshold may be displaced up the runway, temporarily (e.g. works) or permanently
Permanent, arrows before the threshold: the pre-threshold area may be used to taxi and take off, but not to land
Permanent, crosses before the threshold: the area is unfit for any aircraft movement and unsuitable as a stopway
Temporary: chevrons are added, with arrows (taxi and take-off, not landing) or crosses (unfit)
Rule of thumb: arrows = you may roll on it; crosses = keep off it; never land short of the threshold bar
Signals seen only on the ground
Black ball on the mast: take-off and landing directions are not necessarily the same
Two red balls on the mast: gliding in progress
Rectangular red and yellow chequered flag or board: aircraft may move on the manoeuvring area and apron only with ATC permission
Variable circuit: red flag = left-hand, green flag = right-hand
Away from the signals area: a black C on a yellow board marks where to report to ATC or the aerodrome authority
Light signals from ATC
The same light means different things in flight and on the ground
Steady green: in flight, cleared to land; on the ground, cleared to take off (in both cases if you are satisfied there is no risk of collision)
Flashing green: in flight, return to this aerodrome and wait for permission to land; on the ground, cleared to taxi on the manoeuvring area (if no collision risk)
Steady red: in flight, give way to other aircraft and continue circling; on the ground, stop
Flashing red: in flight, do not land, the aerodrome is not available (go elsewhere); on the ground, move clear of the landing area
Red flare (from the ground): do not land for the time being, wait for permission, whatever earlier instructions said
Flashing white: in flight, land here after a steady green, then await further instructions; on the ground, return to your starting point on the aerodrome
Trap: a steady green on the ground is take-off, not taxi; a flashing green is taxi
Light signals from aircraft
Pyrotechnics are rarely carried. The signal nearly any aircraft can make is switching the landing or navigation lights on and off (usually visible only at night)
Flashing landing and/or navigation lights: I am compelled to land
Red flare: immediate assistance required
Green flare: by night, may I land? By day, may I land in a different direction from the one the landing T shows?
Marshalling signals: marshaller to pilot
Move ahead: arms repeatedly moved upward and backward, beckoning
Turn to port (open up starboard engine): right arm down, left arm beckoning. Turn to starboard: left arm down, right arm beckoning. The faster the arm, the tighter the turn
Stop: arms repeatedly crossed above the head; speed shows urgency
Slow down: arms down, palms to the ground, moved up and down. One arm only: slow the engines on that side
Start engine: circular motion of the right hand at head level, the left arm pointing to (or the left hand's fingers showing) the engine
Cut engines: arm and hand level with the chest, moved sideways, palm down
Chocks inserted: arms out, palms in, swung inwards. Chocks away: arms down, palms out, swung outwards
Engage brakes: hand raised in front of the body, fingers out, then fist clenched. Release brakes: fist raised, then fingers extended
This bay: arms vertical above the head. Proceed to the next marshaller: one arm down, the other across the body pointing to them
All clear, marshalling finished: right arm raised at the elbow, palm forward
Back the tail to starboard or port: one arm pointing down, the other repeatedly brought down from overhead to horizontal forward
Marshalling signals: helicopters
Hover: arms horizontal out to the sides
Land: arms down and crossed in front of the body
Move upwards / downwards: arms out to the sides, palms up beckoning up, or palms down beckoning down; speed shows the rate
Move horizontally: one arm out to the side, the other swept across the body towards it, repeated
Move back: arms down, palms forward, swept up to shoulder level and back down
Release load: left arm forward horizontally, right arm slicing horizontally below it
Signals from pilot to marshaller
Brakes engaged: hand raised in front of the face, fingers out, then fist clenched. Brakes released: fist raised, then fingers extended
Insert chocks: arms out, palms out, hands moved in to cross in front of the face. Remove chocks: hands crossed in front of the face, moved outwards
Ready to start: hold up the number of fingers for the engine to be started
Engines are numbered from the marshaller's right to left as they face the aircraft: No. 1 port outer, No. 2 port inner, No. 3 starboard inner, No. 4 starboard outer
Emergency hand signals
Used by the fire and rescue service to the flight crew. At night the same signals are made with wands
Recommend evacuation: one arm out horizontally, hand at eye level, beckoning backwards; the other arm against the body
Recommend stop (halt the evacuation or movement): arms in front of the head, crossed at the wrists
Emergency contained (all clear, nothing dangerous seen outside): arms out and down at 45°, brought in to cross below the waist, then out again
Fire: right hand fanning from shoulder to knee while the left hand points at the fire

sum.What an aerodrome is: Any land or water used for take-off and landing; details are in the AIP AD directory.
sum.Prior permission (PPR) and limits on use: Get permission before departure: from the aerodrome authority, or the owner at unlicensed sites. Military aerodromes have extra limits, lifted in an emergency.
sum.ANO rules at aerodromes: instruction, fu: Adequate facilities for training, fit fuel only, report delays of 45 minutes or more, and customs airports are in AIP GEN.
sum.Security (ICAO Annex 17): Annex 17 aims to prevent unlawful interference; security is everyone's job.
sum.Aeronautical light beacons: Green Morse every 12 seconds is civil, red is military; aerodrome beacons flash white/white or white/green.
sum.Moving on the aerodrome (Rules 12 and 13: You need permission to taxi or to walk onto aircraft areas; the manoeuvring area excludes aprons.
sum.Right of way on the ground (SERA.3210): Give way to landing and departing aircraft; head-on turn right, give way to traffic on your right, overtaker keeps clear. The onus is on you.
sum.Aerodrome Traffic Zones (ATZs): Airspace around busy aerodromes where you must keep radio contact; dimensions in chapter 5.
sum.Declared distances (TORA, TODA, ASDA, LD: TORA is the ground run; add clearway for TODA, stopway for ASDA; LDA is for landing.
sum.Aerodrome standards (ICAO Annex 14): Annex 14 sets aerodrome standards; CAP 637 and CAP 1535 explain them.
sum.Runway surface condition (GRF and SNOWTA: Dry, wet (up to 3 mm), slippery wet or contaminated, reported per third with codes 0 to 6, by SNOWTAM all year.
sum.Indicators, markings and signs (Annex 14: At least one windsock; runway markings white, taxiway yellow; mandatory signs white on red.
sum.Runway lights (Annex 14 5.3): Threshold green towards the approach; end lights red towards the runway.
Vehicles flash yellow, high-intensity lights flash white, small obstacles get one steady red.
sum.Signals area: direction and surfaces: Land towards the T's cross-arm; disc or black ball = directions differ; dumb-bell = hard surfaces.
sum.Signals area: circuit direction and warn: Striped arrow or green flag = right-hand circuit; one yellow diagonal = care, yellow cross = no landing; double cross = gliding.
sum.Signals on paved runways and taxiways: Crosses mark unfit sections; at a holding point the broken lines face the runway.
sum.Markers on unpaved manoeuvring areas: Orange/white wedges 45 m apart = boundary; flat white 90 m apart = runway edge; crosses at the ends = storage or emergency only.
sum.Displaced thresholds: Arrows before the threshold = taxi and take-off but no landing; crosses = unfit.
sum.Signals seen only on the ground: Black ball, two red balls, chequered board (ATC permission to move), red/green flags, black C for reporting.
sum.Light signals from ATC: Green steady: land or take off; green flashing: return or taxi; red steady: circle or stop; red flashing: don't land or clear the runway; white flashing: land after green or go back.
sum.Light signals from aircraft: Flashing lights = compelled to land; red flare = help; green flare = may I land (by day: in another direction).
sum.Marshalling signals: marshaller to pilot: Beckon = come ahead; one arm down = turn the other way; crossed above head = stop.
sum.Marshalling signals: helicopters: Arms out = hover, crossed low = land, palms show up or down.
sum.Signals from pilot to marshaller: Fist and open hand for brakes, crossed hands for chocks; engines numbered from the marshaller's right.
sum.Emergency hand signals: Evacuate, stop, contained, fire: the four fire-crew signals.

cards.q: Which AIP section is the aerodrome directory?
cards.a: AD (Aerodromes): characteristics, local hazards and restrictions.

cards.q: Who gives permission to land at a military or ordinary-licence aerodrome?
cards.a: The aerodrome authority (prior permission, PPR).

cards.q: Who gives permission to land at an unlicensed aerodrome?
cards.a: The owner or person in charge.

cards.q: When should you get PPR?
cards.a: Before departure, especially if no radio frequency is published.

cards.q: Two consequences of landing without PPR?
cards.a: It is trespass, and an insurer may refuse a claim because you breached the ANO (plus you miss safety information).

cards.q: What limits civil use of military aerodromes?
cards.a: Normal hours of watch and inland flights only; some limit the class of traffic. Not in an emergency.

cards.q: Can you land at an aerodrome not in AIP AD?
cards.a: Yes, in an emergency or with the owner's or operator's permission.

cards.q: Flying instruction at an unlicensed aerodrome: who must be satisfied?
cards.a: The operator that the facilities are adequate, and the commander before take-off (Article 209).

cards.q: What does Article 220 say about fuel?
cards.a: Do not use fuel you know or suspect is unfit; it must be stored and sampled as required.

cards.q: What colour marks Avgas equipment?
cards.a: Red, usually.

cards.q: When must you tell your destination you are late?
cards.a: As soon as possible if you will be 45 minutes or more late, or change destination.

cards.q: Where are customs airports listed?
cards.a: AIP GEN, with hours and special requirements.

cards.q: Which ICAO Annex covers security?
cards.a: Annex 17.

cards.q: Green Morse identification beacon?
cards.a: Civil aerodrome: two-letter group every 12 seconds.

cards.q: Red Morse identification beacon?
cards.a: Military aerodrome: two-letter group every 12 seconds.

cards.q: Alternating white/white or white/green flashes?
cards.a: An aerodrome beacon (civil).

cards.q: When are light beacons usually on?
cards.a: At night, and by day in poor visibility, while the aerodrome is operating.

cards.q: Manoeuvring area vs apron?
cards.a: Manoeuvring area: take-off, landing and taxiing (no aprons). Apron: loading, turn-rounds and maintenance.

cards.q: What do you need before taxiing on the apron or manoeuvring area?
cards.a: The aerodrome authority's permission.

cards.q: On the ground, who gives way to aircraft taking off or landing?
cards.a: Everyone on the ground.

cards.q: Two aircraft taxi head-on. What does each do?
cards.a: Turn right.

cards.q: Converging while taxiing: who gives way?
cards.a: The one with the other on its right: stop or pass behind.

cards.q: Overtaking while taxiing: who has right of way?
cards.a: The aircraft being overtaken. The overtaker keeps clear until past and well clear.

cards.q: Why is an ATZ established?
cards.a: Usually because of the amount of flying around the aerodrome.

cards.q: What does TORA mean?
cards.a: Take-off run available: runway declared suitable for the ground run of a take-off.

cards.q: TODA = ?
cards.a: TORA plus clearway (if provided).

cards.q: ASDA = ?
cards.a: TORA plus stopway (if provided). No stopway: ASDA = TORA.

cards.q: What is LDA?
cards.a: Landing distance available: runway declared suitable for the landing ground run.

cards.q: What is a stopway?
cards.a: A prepared area beyond the runway end, in the take-off direction, for stopping after an abandoned take-off.

cards.q: Which Annex covers aerodromes?
cards.a: ICAO Annex 14.

cards.q: Wet runway: how deep can the water be?
cards.a: Up to and including 3 mm.

cards.q: When is a runway third reported as contaminated?
cards.a: When more than 25% of it is covered by a contaminant.

cards.q: Runway condition code range?
cards.a: 0 (worst) to 6 (best), one for each runway third.

cards.q: What carries GRF runway reports, even for standing water?
cards.a: A SNOWTAM.

cards.q: Which runway number does a SNOWTAM give?
cards.a: The lower one (09 for runway 09/27).

cards.q: Colour of runway and taxiway markings?
cards.a: Runway white, taxiway and stand markings yellow.

cards.q: Colour of mandatory instruction signs?
cards.a: White on a red background.

cards.q: Threshold lights?
cards.a: Fixed, unidirectional, green towards the approach.

cards.q: Runway end lights?
cards.a: Fixed, unidirectional, red towards the runway; ideally at least six, no more than 3 m beyond the end.

cards.q: Obstacle light on a vehicle (not emergency)?
cards.a: Flashing yellow (low intensity).

cards.q: Small obstacle (45 m or less) lit how?
cards.a: A single steady red light on its highest point.

cards.q: White T in the signals area?
cards.a: Take off and land parallel with the shaft, towards the cross-arm.

cards.q: White disc at the head of the T (or black ball on the mast)?
cards.a: Landing and take-off directions do not necessarily coincide.

cards.q: White dumb-bell?
cards.a: Keep to hard surfaces on the ground.

cards.q: Dumb-bell with black strips across the discs?
cards.a: Take off and land on a runway; other ground movement need not be on hard surfaces.

cards.q: Red and yellow striped arrow bent clockwise?
cards.a: Right-hand circuit.

cards.q: Red flag / green flag on the signals mast?
cards.a: Left-hand circuit / right-hand circuit.

cards.q: Red square, one yellow diagonal?
cards.a: Manoeuvring area in poor state: take special care landing.

cards.q: Red square, yellow diagonal cross?
cards.a: Landing prohibited, likely for a long time.

cards.q: Double white cross or two red balls?
cards.a: Glider flying in progress.

cards.q: Yellow cross on the aerodrome?
cards.a: Tow-rope dropping area.

cards.q: Crosses on a runway (white) or taxiway (yellow)?
cards.a: That section is unfit for aircraft; crosses no more than 300 m apart.

cards.q: Holding point: which lines face the runway?
cards.a: The broken lines.

cards.q: Orange and white wedges 45 m apart?
cards.a: Aerodrome boundary (unpaved).

cards.q: Flat white rectangles 90 m apart?
cards.a: Boundary of an unpaved runway or stopway.

cards.q: White cross at each end of a runway?
cards.a: Landing dangerous; storage only.

cards.q: White cross plus a white bar at each end?
cards.a: Disused aerodrome: emergency use only.

cards.q: Arrows before a displaced threshold?
cards.a: Pre-threshold area usable for taxi and take-off, not landing.

cards.q: Crosses before a displaced threshold?
cards.a: Pre-threshold area unfit for any movement.

cards.q: Red and yellow chequered flag or board?
cards.a: Move on the manoeuvring area and apron only with ATC permission.

cards.q: Black C on a yellow board?
cards.a: Where to report to ATC or the aerodrome authority.

cards.q: Steady green: in flight / on the ground?
cards.a: Cleared to land / cleared to take off.

cards.q: Flashing green: in flight / on the ground?
cards.a: Return and wait for permission to land / cleared to taxi.

cards.q: Steady red: in flight / on the ground?
cards.a: Give way and keep circling / stop.

cards.q: Flashing red: in flight / on the ground?
cards.a: Do not land, aerodrome not available / move clear of the landing area.

cards.q: Flashing white: in flight / on the ground?
cards.a: Land here after a steady green, then await instructions / return to starting point.

cards.q: Aircraft flashing its landing or nav lights?
cards.a: I am compelled to land.

cards.q: Green flare from an aircraft by day?
cards.a: May I land in a different direction from the landing T?

cards.q: Marshaller: arms repeatedly crossed above the head?
cards.a: Stop (speed shows urgency).

cards.q: Marshaller: right arm raised at the elbow, palm forward?
cards.a: All clear, marshalling finished.

cards.q: How are engines numbered for the marshaller?
cards.a: From the marshaller's right to left: No. 1 port outer to No. 4 starboard outer.

cards.q: Emergency signal: arms crossed at the wrists in front of the head?
cards.a: Recommend stop.

quiz.q: At a civil aerodrome, what does the identification beacon show?
o: A green two-letter Morse group every 12 seconds
A red two-letter Morse group every 12 seconds
A green two-letter Morse group every 10 seconds
quiz.why: Green Morse every 12 seconds is civil. Red is military, and alternating white/green is an aerodrome beacon, not an identification beacon.

quiz.q: You see a red two-letter Morse group flashed from the ground. What is it?
o: A warning that you are entering a danger area
quiz.why: Red Morse identifiers are military; civil ones are green. Danger-area warnings are red and green stars fired every 10 seconds.

quiz.q: What does an aerodrome beacon usually show?
quiz.why: Usually white/white, less often white/green. It is not normally fitted as well as an identification beacon.

quiz.q: How often does an identification beacon flash its Morse group?
quiz.why: Every 12 seconds. The 10-second interval belongs to the red and green warning stars.

quiz.q: You are expected at another aerodrome. When must you tell them you are running late?
o: If you will be 15 minutes or more late
If you will be 30 minutes or more late
If you will be 45 minutes or more late
quiz.why: Forty-five minutes or more, or any change of destination, as soon as possible, so nobody starts overdue action.

quiz.q: Who gives permission to land at an unlicensed aerodrome?
o: The owner or person in charge
quiz.why: The owner or person in charge. At military and ordinary-licence aerodromes it is the aerodrome authority.

quiz.q: When should you get PPR?
quiz.why: Before you set off, especially where no radio frequency is published.

quiz.q: Civil use of a military aerodrome is normally restricted to:
o: Its normal hours of watch and aircraft on inland flights
quiz.why: Normal hours of watch and inland flights, sometimes also by class of traffic. These limits do not apply in an emergency.

quiz.q: Can you land at an aerodrome that is not listed in AIP AD?
o: In an emergency, or with the owner's or operator's permission
quiz.why: Yes, in an emergency or with the owner's or operator's permission.

quiz.q: Before flying instruction towards a licence at an unlicensed aerodrome, who must be satisfied that the facilities are adequate?
o: Both the aerodrome operator and the commander
quiz.why: Article 209: the operator must be satisfied, and the commander must not take off unless they are too.

quiz.q: What colour is Avgas equipment at aerodromes usually marked?
quiz.why: Red. Black is the usual marking for Jet A-1, a common trap.

quiz.q: Where are the UK customs airports for international flights listed?
quiz.why: AIP GEN, with hours of attendance and special requirements.

quiz.q: Which ICAO Annex covers aviation security?
quiz.why: Annex 17. Annex 2 is rules of the air, Annex 11 air traffic services, Annex 14 aerodromes.

quiz.q: What is the manoeuvring area of an aerodrome?
o: The part used for take-off, landing and taxiing, excluding aprons
quiz.why: Take-off, landing and taxiing, but not aprons or maintenance areas. Add the aprons and you have the movement area.

quiz.q: What is an apron used for?
quiz.why: Aprons are for loading, unloading, turn-rounds, maintenance and repair: anything other than flight operations.

quiz.q: You are taxiing and an aircraft is landing. Who gives way?
o: Whichever is on the other's right
quiz.why: Aircraft on the ground give way to those taking off or landing.

quiz.q: Two aircraft are taxiing head-on. What does each do?
o: The one on the taxiway centreline holds course
quiz.why: Each turns right, the same as in the air.

quiz.q: You are taxiing and another aircraft converges from your right. What do you do?
o: Continue: you have right of way
Give way, stopping or passing behind it
quiz.why: It is on your right, so you give way and avoid crossing ahead unless well clear.

quiz.q: You are taxiing faster than an aircraft ahead of you on the same taxiway. Who has right of way?
quiz.why: The aircraft being overtaken. As the overtaker you keep out of the way until past and well clear.

quiz.q: ATC has cleared you to taxi, but a vehicle pulls out ahead. Whose duty is it to avoid a collision?
o: Whoever is on the other's right
quiz.why: Regardless of any ATC clearance, the commander must do everything possible to avoid a collision on the ground.

quiz.q: Whose permission do you need to taxi on an apron?
quiz.why: The aerodrome authority's permission is needed for the apron and the manoeuvring area (Rule 12).

quiz.q: Apart from trespass, what risk do you run by landing without PPR?
o: Your insurer may refuse a claim because you breached the ANO
quiz.why: You may miss safety information and, after an accident, the insurer may refuse to pay because you breached the ANO.

quiz.q: You told your destination you were coming. You are now running 50 minutes late. What must you do?
o: Tell that aerodrome as soon as possible
Nothing, unless the delay reaches 60 minutes
quiz.why: Tell them as soon as possible if you change destination or will be 45 minutes or more late, so they do not start overdue action. 60 and 30 minutes are the usual distractors.

quiz.q: Which is the take-off run available (TORA)?
o: The runway declared suitable for the ground run of an aeroplane taking off
The runway declared suitable for the take-off ground run, plus any clearway
quiz.why: TORA is the ground-run length only. Adding the clearway gives TODA; adding the stopway gives ASDA.

quiz.q: Which declared distance includes the clearway?
quiz.why: TODA = TORA + clearway. The stopway belongs to ASDA, not TODA.

quiz.q: A runway has no stopway. What is its ASDA?
quiz.why: ASDA = TORA + stopway, so with no stopway it equals TORA.

quiz.q: A runway third has standing water covering 20% of it. How is that third reported?
o: Not contaminated: coverage must be more than 25%
Contaminated, because there is standing water
Contaminated if it is deeper than 3 mm
quiz.why: A third is contaminated only when more than a quarter of it is covered. Depth alone does not make it contaminated.

quiz.q: Up to what depth of water is a runway reported as wet rather than contaminated?
o: Up to 3 mm, not including 3 mm
quiz.why: Wet = visible dampness or water up to and including 3 mm (given enough coverage, deeper water is a contaminant).

quiz.q: In the GRF, a runway condition code of 0 means:
quiz.why: Codes run from 0 (worst) to 6 (best).

quiz.q: Standing water is reported on a runway in July. How is it notified?
o: It is not notified outside winter
quiz.why: The GRF runs all year; a SNOWTAM reports standing water too, not only snow and ice.

quiz.q: A SNOWTAM shows 09 for runway 09/27 with 27 in use. Why?
o: SNOWTAMs give the lower runway number
It is the runway condition code
quiz.why: The lower designator is always given; the report covers the runway whichever way it is used.

quiz.q: ICAO recommends which marking colours?
o: White on runways, yellow on taxiways
Yellow on runways, white on taxiways
Blue on runways, yellow on taxiways
quiz.why: Runway markings white; taxiway and stand markings yellow.

quiz.q: Runway threshold lights are:
o: Fixed green, showing towards the approach
Fixed green, showing along the runway
Fixed white, showing towards the approach
quiz.why: Fixed unidirectional green towards the approach. The red end lights are the ones that face along the runway.

quiz.q: Runway end lights show:
quiz.why: Fixed unidirectional red in the direction of the runway, ideally at least six of them.

quiz.q: A mandatory instruction sign is:
quiz.why: White inscription on a red background.

quiz.q: A tug towing an airliner shows a low-intensity obstacle light. What colour?
quiz.why: Ordinary vehicles flash yellow. Emergency and security vehicles are excepted; high-intensity obstacle lights flash white.

quiz.q: How is a 40 m mast near an aerodrome normally lit at night?
o: A single steady red light at the top
A flashing white light at the top
Red lights outlining its whole height
quiz.why: Fixed obstacles 45 m or less in height, width and length get one steady red light at the highest point.

quiz.q: In the signals area you see a white T with a white disc at the head. It means:
o: Landing and take-off directions do not necessarily coincide
The manoeuvring area is in poor state
quiz.why: The disc (or a black ball on the mast) warns that the two directions may differ.

quiz.q: You land using the white T in the signals area. Which way do you land?
o: Parallel with the shaft, towards the cross-arm
Parallel with the shaft, away from the cross-arm
quiz.why: Towards the cross-arm, i.e. into wind, unless ATC say otherwise.

quiz.q: A white dumb-bell with a black strip across each disc means:
o: Take off and land on a runway, but ground movement need not be on hard surfaces
Use hard surfaces only, on the ground and for take-off and landing
Light aircraft may use the grass
quiz.why: Plain dumb-bell: hard surfaces only on the ground. The black strips relax that for taxiing but keep take-off and landing on the runway.

quiz.q: A red and yellow striped arrow, bent clockwise round the edge of the signals area, means:
quiz.why: Turns before landing and after take-off are to the right.

quiz.q: A green rectangular flag flies from the signals mast. The circuit is:
quiz.why: Green = right-hand, red = left-hand, as with nav lights (green starboard, red port).

quiz.q: A red square with a single yellow diagonal means:
o: The manoeuvring area is poor: take special care on approach and landing
quiz.why: One diagonal = take special care. A yellow diagonal cross = landing prohibited.

quiz.q: A red square with a yellow diagonal cross means:
o: Landing prohibited, likely to be prolonged
quiz.why: The cross means landing is prohibited. A single diagonal only calls for special care; a yellow cross alone is the tow-rope area.

quiz.q: Two red balls hang one above the other on the signals mast. This means:
o: Landing and take-off directions may differ
quiz.why: Two red balls (or a double white cross) = gliding. One black ball = directions may differ.

quiz.q: Crosses with arms at 45° to the centreline appear on a taxiway. What colour are they and what do they mean?
o: Yellow; that section is unfit for aircraft
White; that section is unfit for aircraft
quiz.why: Yellow on a taxiway, white on a runway, no more than 300 m apart.

quiz.q: You have landed and are vacating the runway. You meet two broken yellow lines, then two continuous ones. Do you need a clearance to cross?
o: No: you meet the broken lines first, so you are leaving the runway side
Yes, because the continuous lines are beyond
quiz.why: The broken lines face the runway. Approaching from the runway, the holding point does not need a clearance.

quiz.q: Taxiing out towards the runway, you reach a holding point with continuous lines on your side. What applies?
o: Do not cross without ATC permission
Cross if you see no traffic
quiz.why: No part of the aircraft may pass the holding point towards the runway without permission.

quiz.q: Orange and white wedge-shaped markers no more than 45 m apart show:
o: The edge of an unpaved runway
An unfit part of a paved runway
quiz.why: Wedges mark the boundary (or, alternating with flags, an unserviceable unpaved area). Unpaved runway edges are flat white markers 90 m apart.

quiz.q: Flat white rectangles flush with the ground, no more than 90 m apart, mark:
o: The boundary of an unpaved runway or stopway
quiz.why: Flat white = runway or stopway edge. Orange and white wedges at 45 m = aerodrome boundary.

quiz.q: A white cross and a single white bar at each end of a runway at a disused aerodrome means:
quiz.why: Cross plus bar = emergency only (and the runway is not safeguarded). A cross alone = dangerous, storage only.

quiz.q: Before a permanently displaced threshold there are white arrows. The area may be used for:
quiz.why: Arrows = usable for taxi and take-off. Crosses would mean unfit for any movement.

quiz.q: On the ground you see a red and yellow chequered board. It means:
o: Move on the manoeuvring area and apron only with ATC permission
quiz.why: Chequered = ATC permission needed to move. A black C on yellow shows where to report.

quiz.q: A steady red light is aimed at you (i) in flight and (ii) on the ground. It means:
o: (i) Give way to other aircraft and continue circling (ii) stop
(i) Aerodrome closed (ii) return to starting point
(i) Wait for permission to land (ii) cleared to take off
(i) Do not land (ii) move clear of the landing area
quiz.why: Steady red: keep circling, or stop. Flashing red means aerodrome unavailable, or move clear of the landing area.

quiz.q: Holding at the runway, you get a steady green light. It means:
o: Cleared to take off, if no collision risk
Cleared to cross the runway only
quiz.why: Steady green on the ground is take-off. A flashing green is taxi.

quiz.q: Flying near the aerodrome with a radio failure, you see green flashes from the tower. They mean:
o: Return to this aerodrome and wait for permission to land
quiz.why: Flashing green in flight = come back and wait; steady green = cleared to land.

quiz.q: You are taxiing and receive a series of white flashes. You should:
o: Return to your starting point on the aerodrome
Move clear of the landing area
quiz.why: Flashing white on the ground = return to starting point. In flight it means land here after a steady green, then await instructions.

quiz.q: In flight you see a flashing red light from the tower. You should:
o: Not land: the aerodrome is not available
quiz.why: Flashing red in flight = do not land here. Steady red = give way and keep circling.

quiz.q: At night, a pilot flashes the landing lights on and off over the aerodrome. This means:
quiz.why: Flashing landing or nav lights = compelled to land. A green flare by night asks 'may I land?', a red flare asks for immediate help.

quiz.q: By day, an aircraft fires a green flare. It asks:
o: May I land in a different direction from that shown by the landing T?
quiz.why: By night a green flare asks 'may I land?'; by day it asks to land in a different direction from the T.

quiz.q: A marshaller holds the right arm down and repeatedly beckons with the left arm. You should:
quiz.why: Right arm down, left arm beckoning = turn to port (open up the starboard engine). The faster the arm, the tighter the turn.

quiz.q: A marshaller raises the right arm at the elbow, palm facing forwards. It means:
quiz.why: All clear. Arms crossed above the head is stop; both arms vertical is 'this bay'.

quiz.q: The marshaller faces a four-engined aircraft. Which is No. 1 engine?
quiz.why: Numbering runs from the marshaller's right to left: No. 1 port outer, through to No. 4 starboard outer.

quiz.q: A fire crew member crosses both arms at the wrists in front of the head. It means:
quiz.why: Arms crossed in front of the head = recommend stop. Arms swept down and crossed below the waist = emergency contained.

quiz.q: Which ICAO Annex sets the standards for aerodromes?
quiz.why: Annex 14 is aerodromes. Annex 17 is security, Annex 2 the rules of the air, Annex 11 air traffic services.

quiz.q: Taxiing on the manoeuvring area, ATC have cleared you along a taxiway and another aircraft approaches head-on. Who must avoid the collision?
o: You, as commander, whatever the clearance
The aircraft with the greater speed
quiz.why: The commander must do everything possible to avoid a collision regardless of ATC. Head-on, both turn right.
